title: Querying Logs with Loki and LogQL
intro: Loki indexes only labels (app, namespace, pod), not full log text, which makes it cheap to run. LogQL queries start by selecting streams by label, then filter their content.

steps.prompt: Pull recent logs from every stream labeled app=checkout-service.
steps.explanation: The stream selector {app="checkout-service"} picks logs across every pod with that label.
steps.why: Unlike kubectl logs, Loki keeps logs after pods are deleted or rescheduled — essential when the pod that failed no longer exists by the time you investigate.

steps.explanation: |= keeps lines containing the string; != excludes them; |~ matches a regex.
steps.why: Always narrow with the label selector first, then the line filter. Loki only indexes labels, so a broad selector with a text filter scans far more data and is slow.

steps.prompt: Parse JSON-formatted logs and keep only lines where status_code is 500.
steps.explanation: | json extracts every JSON field as a label you can filter on.
steps.why: Structured (JSON) logging pays off here: filtering on an exact field is precise, while grepping for '500' also matches durations, IDs, and anything else containing those digits.

steps.prompt: Turn logs into a metric: the rate of error lines per second over 5 minutes.
steps.why: LogQL metric queries let you graph and alert on log patterns in Grafana — useful for services that don't expose Prometheus metrics at all.
